notes: Ruling slot 18 = Supreme Revolutionary Council (Siad Barre). Coalition slot 19 filled with the scientific-socialist ideologues inside the regime (catchy). SYL placed in slot 0 as Egal's Western-leaning governing party deposed in Oct 1969. All parties banned since the coup; descriptions reflect that. Greater Somalia League in 20 (has popularity). Shia slots use small Indian Shia trading communities of Mogadishu.

0.name: Ururka Dhallinyarada Soomaaliyeed
0.text:
The Somali Youth League led the country to independence in 1960 and dominated every parliament since. After President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke was assassinated in October 1969, the army seized power on 21 October, dissolved the National Assembly and banned the party. Prime Minister Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal and much of the leadership are now in detention.

Under Egal the SYL sought détente with Kenya and Ethiopia, close ties with Italy, Britain and the United States, and Western aid for development. Its strength lay in clan patronage networks, the civil service and urban notables, many of whom still quietly expect the soldiers to hand power back.

1.name: Somali National League
1.text:
The Somali National League was the leading party of the former British Somaliland Protectorate and carried the north into union with the south in 1960. Most of its leaders, Egal among them, later merged into the governing Somali Youth League, but its Hargeisa and Berbera notables remain a distinct northern bloc, now silenced by the October 1969 coup.

The League stands for constitutional government, the rule of law inherited from British administration, free trade through Berbera and a fair share of power for the north. It looks to Britain and the West, and its leverage lies with Isaaq merchants, livestock exporters and northern civil servants.

2.name: Dastuuriyiinta
2.text:
The Constitutionalists are the reform-minded civilians of the parliamentary era who defended the 1960 constitution and clean government. Their figureheads are former President Aden Abdullah Osman, who peacefully handed over power in 1967, and former Prime Minister Abdirazak Haji Hussein, known for his campaign against corruption and now held by the junta.

They want the soldiers back in their barracks, a restored parliament, independent courts and a free press. They favour cooperation with Western donors without dependence on any bloc. Their base is the educated elite, lawyers and teachers of Mogadishu, and their leverage is the moral prestige of the only Somali head of state who ever stepped down voluntarily.

3.name: Midowga Dimoqraadiga Soomaaliyeed
3.text:
The Somali Democratic Union was formed in 1962 as a left-leaning opposition to the dominant Somali Youth League. It contested the parliamentary elections of the 1960s with a programme of social reform but never broke the SYL's clan-based machine, and like every other party it was dissolved by the Supreme Revolutionary Council in October 1969.

The Union favours planned development, labour rights, land reform along the Shabelle and Juba rivers and an end to clan patronage, within a parliamentary framework. It draws on teachers, clerks and trade unionists in Mogadishu and Kismayo. Many of its sympathisers now hesitate between opposing military rule and serving the junta's socialist rhetoric.

4.name: Ardayda Moskow
4.text:
The Moscow Graduates are the officers and cadets trained in Soviet military academies since the USSR began arming the Somali National Army in 1963. Hundreds of them returned with Russian, Marxist-Leninist textbooks and a taste for vanguard politics, and they formed the backbone of the October 1969 coup that brought the Supreme Revolutionary Council to power.

They want a disciplined Leninist party, nationalisation of banks and trade, collective farms and a formal alliance with Moscow. They distrust clan elders, sheikhs and the old politicians alike. Their leverage lies in the officer corps, the Soviet advisers attached to every major unit and the arms pipeline on which the army depends.

5.name: Halgan
5.text:
Halgan is the radical student milieu of the University Institute of Mogadishu and the secondary schools of the capital, where pamphlets from Cairo, Peking and Paris circulate alongside the new Somali-language poetry. The students cheered the fall of the old politicians in October 1969 but already suspect the officers of wanting obedience rather than revolution.

They demand immediate abolition of clan privileges, a written Somali script, mass literacy campaigns and support for liberation movements across Africa. They reject both Western patronage and Soviet tutelage. Their leverage is their energy in street mobilisation and the junta's need for educated cadres to staff its new ministries.

6.name: Calanka Buluugga
6.text:
The Blue Flag is the hardline irredentist current among officers and nationalist veterans who never accepted Egal's détente with Ethiopia and Kenya. Named after the national flag whose five-pointed star stands for the five Somali territories, it regards the 1967 Arusha understanding with Kenya as treason and the Ogaden as occupied land.

Its members want to reunite all Somalis by force and will take arms from anyone who offers them, above all the Soviet Union, since Washington backs Addis Ababa. They are hostile to Western influence and to compromise with neighbours. Their leverage rests with field commanders, Ogaden refugees and the nomadic clans living astride the borders.

7.name: Booliska Soomaaliyeed
7.text:
The Somali Police Force is the country's oldest uniformed institution and a full partner in the October 1969 takeover. Its commander, General Jama Ali Korshel, serves as a vice-president of the Supreme Revolutionary Council, and police officers sit beside soldiers in the regime's committees and new security courts.

The police leadership wants order before ideology: tight control of the press, detention of the old politicians and surveillance of clan and religious networks. It is wary of both Soviet advisers and Western embassies, preferring a strong Somali state answerable to its own officers. Its leverage lies in its nationwide presence, intelligence files and control of the capital's streets.

8.name: Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat of Mogadishu
8.text:
The Dawoodi Bohra Jamaat of Mogadishu is the small Shia trading community of Gujarati origin that settled in the Benadir ports during the colonial era. Organised around its mosque and community hall, it follows the spiritual authority of the Da'i al-Mutlaq in Bombay and keeps a low political profile under the new military government.

The community values education, commerce and peaceful coexistence with the Sunni majority. It favours stable property rights and open trade routes to India and the Gulf, and fears the nationalisation of import houses. Its leverage is modest but real: credit, shipping contacts and a share of the capital's wholesale trade.

9.name: Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat of Mogadishu
9.english: Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat of Mogadishu
9.text:
The Khoja Shia Ithna'ashari Jamaat of Mogadishu is a handful of Twelver Shia families of Indian origin, linked to the East African federation of Khoja communities based in Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar. Their religious guidance comes from the senior clerics of Najaf, whose students occasionally pass through the East African coast.

Within this tiny circle, a stricter devotional milieu holds that political authority belongs ultimately to the learned jurists and rejects both secular socialism and Western mores. It has no foothold among Somalis, and its influence rests entirely on religious networks across the Indian Ocean and the commercial standing of its members.

10.name: Dariiqada Qaadiriya
10.text:
The Qadiriyya is the oldest and most widespread Sufi brotherhood in Somalia, with religious settlements, shrines and teachers spread from Benadir to the north. Alongside the Ahmadiyya and Salihiyya orders it shapes the faith of most Somalis, and its sheikhs mediate disputes, run Quranic schools and preside over the great pilgrimages to saints' tombs.

The order stands for established Islam, respect for elders and sharia in family life, and it is deeply wary of the junta's secular and socialist talk. It avoids open confrontation and favours accommodation with whoever rules. Its leverage lies in the loyalty of rural communities and its central place in Somali religious life.

11.name: Wahdat al-Shabab al-Islami
11.text:
Unity of Islamic Youth was founded in Hargeisa in 1969 by young northerners returning from studies in Saudi Arabia and Egypt. It rejects the Sufi orders as innovation and preaches a purified Islam based directly on the Quran and Sunna. Since the October coup it operates quietly through mosques and study circles.

The group wants Somalia governed by Islamic law rather than imported ideologies, and sees the junta's socialist rhetoric and Soviet advisers as a threat to the faith. Its members are students, teachers and young traders with links to the Arabian Peninsula. Its leverage is small but growing, carried by Gulf scholarships and remittances.

12.name: Jamaacada Ahli
12.text:
The Al-Ahli Group took shape in Mogadishu in 1969 among students and graduates inspired by the Muslim Brotherhood ideas brought home from al-Azhar, above all through the teaching of Sheikh Mohamed Moallim Hassan. It works through lectures, study groups and charitable activity rather than as a formal party, and stays cautious under military rule.

It calls for an Islamic social order, moral reform of public life and Arabic and Islamic education, while accepting modern institutions. It opposes atheist communism and Western cultural influence alike. Its base is urban youth, teachers and civil servants, and its leverage lies in its links to Egyptian and Sudanese religious circles.

13.name: Golaha Xoghayayaasha
13.text:
The Council of Secretaries is the civilian cabinet appointed by the Supreme Revolutionary Council in November 1969 to run the ministries. Its members are mostly educated professionals without party backgrounds, such as the foreign secretary Omar Arteh Ghalib, chosen to give the military government administrative competence and international respectability.

The secretaries favour efficient administration, planned development and a non-aligned foreign policy that keeps aid flowing from East and West. They have no independent power base and serve at the pleasure of the officers, but their expertise in finance, diplomacy and planning makes them indispensable to a junta with little experience of governing.

14.name: Hizbia Dastur Mustaqil Somali
14.text:
The Somali Independent Constitutional Party grew out of the Hizbia Digil Mirifle, the party of the agro-pastoral clans of the inter-riverine south around Baidoa. It was the main regional opposition to the Somali Youth League through the 1950s and 1960s until the junta dissolved all parties in October 1969.

The party stands for a federal constitution, protection of the farming clans' land and a fair share of offices for the south-west against the dominance of the large nomadic clans. It is socially conservative and wary of both Soviet and Western entanglement. Its leverage lies with Digil and Mirifle elders and the farmers of the Bay region.

15.name: Società Agricola Italo-Somala
15.text:
The Italo-Somali Agricultural Society was founded in 1920 by the Duke of the Abruzzi and runs the great sugar and banana estates of Jowhar on the Shabelle river. Together with the Italian banana planters and the import houses of Mogadishu, it represents the colonial-era capital that still dominates the modern economy.

Its managers want guaranteed access to the Italian market, cheap labour and protection from expropriation. They dread the junta's talk of socialism, which threatens nationalisation of banks, plantations and foreign trade. Their leverage lies in export earnings, the jobs of thousands of riverine farm workers and Rome's influence as Somalia's largest Western donor.

16.name: Suuqa Xamarweyne
16.text:
The Hamarweyne Market stands for the Somali traders of Mogadishu's old quarter and their counterparts in Berbera, Kismayo and Bosaso, who live from livestock exports to Arabia, imports and money transfers. They prospered under the open economy of the parliamentary years and watch the new junta with growing unease.

The merchants want free prices, open ports, low taxes and freedom to trade with Aden, Jeddah and Nairobi. They oppose state monopolies, cooperatives imposed from above and any controls on hard currency. Their leverage is economic: they feed the cities, finance clan politics and can move goods and money beyond the reach of the state.

17.name: Xeerka Daaqa
17.text:
The Grazing Law refers to the customary rules by which Somali clans share pasture and water, enforced by elders and religious men. Its defenders are nomadic elders and range experts alarmed by overgrazing around new boreholes, the spread of private enclosures and the felling of acacia woodland for the charcoal trade to Arabia.

They want communal grazing reserves, controls on charcoal burning, careful placement of wells and respect for the seasonal movement of herds. Suspicious of foreign development schemes, they see protection of the land as protection of the Somali way of life. Their leverage lies with the herding majority of the population and the elders who speak for it.

18.name: Golaha Sare ee Kacaanka
18.text:
The Supreme Revolutionary Council is the military body that took power on 21 October 1969, days after the assassination of President Shermarke. Headed by Major General Mohamed Siad Barre, commander of the army, it suspended the constitution, dissolved parliament and the parties and renamed the country the Somali Democratic Republic.

The Council promises to end tribalism, corruption and nepotism, to build a self-reliant socialist economy and to unite all Somalis. It courts Soviet military aid while remaining in the Non-Aligned Movement and the Arab world's orbit. Its power rests on the army, the police and the popular disgust with the corrupt parliamentary order it overthrew.

19.name: Hantiwadaag
19.text:
Hantiwadaag, the Somali word for socialism, is the rallying cry of the civilian ideologues around the new regime. Intellectuals such as Mohamed Aden Sheikh, a member of the Council of Secretaries, urge the officers to give their revolution a coherent Marxist doctrine adapted to Somali conditions rather than to copy any foreign model.

They call for a Somali scientific socialism: a vanguard party, cooperatives, mass literacy, the emancipation of women and the replacement of clan loyalty with loyalty to the nation. They welcome Soviet and Chinese aid but insist on Somali control. Their leverage is ideological: they write the slogans, the curricula and the speeches the junta needs.

20.name: Greater Somalia League
20.text:
The Greater Somalia League was founded in 1958 by Haji Mohamed Hussein after he broke with the Somali Youth League. It became the loudest voice of pan-Somali irredentism and of closer ties with Nasser's Egypt and the Arab world, and it remained a militant opposition party until the junta dissolved it in October 1969.

The League demands the union of the Ogaden, the Northern Frontier District of Kenya and Djibouti with the republic, and rejects all compromise with Addis Ababa and Nairobi. It denounces Western influence and old-party corruption alike. Its base is urban youth, nationalist veterans and refugees from the lost territories.

21.name: Gaashaanka Kacaanka
21.text:
Shield of the Revolution is the hardline core of officers and security men who want the October revolution made permanent and absolute. They see the detention of the old politicians as only a beginning and look to their commander, Siad Barre, as the father of the nation whose word should be beyond question.

They favour revolutionary courts, mass mobilisation in uniform, a cult of the leader and the suppression of clan elders, religious critics and liberal intellectuals. Their nationalism is total: one nation, one leader, one revolution. Their leverage lies in their closeness to the head of state and in their growing hold on detentions and interrogations.

22.name: Xoogga Dalka Soomaaliyeed
22.text:
The Somali National Army was formed at independence from the colonial Somali units and has grown, with Soviet weapons and training since 1963, into one of the larger armies of sub-Saharan Africa. It fought Ethiopia in 1964, and on 21 October 1969 it took power, with Siad Barre and officers such as Mohamed Ali Samatar at the head of the new order.

The officer corps sees itself as the only truly national institution, above clan and party. It wants modern arms, discipline and a free hand to rebuild the state. Its leverage is decisive: it controls the government, the capital and the guns on which every faction depends.

23.name: Boqortooyada Majeerteen
23.text:
The Majeerteen Sultanate ruled the north-eastern horn from Aluula and Bargal until Italian forces annexed it in 1927. The dynasty of Boqor Osman Mahamuud survives as a house of traditional dignitaries, and alongside it the titled sultans and ugaas of other clans still preside over customary assemblies across the country.

The traditional rulers stand for clan custom, the authority of lineage and Islam, and the dignity of hereditary office. They distrusted the party politicians and now face a junta that denounces tribalism. Their leverage lies in their role in resolving feuds, their religious legitimacy and the deference rural Somalis still pay to titled elders.
